newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican president defends himself for backing PRI.
newsitem.headline: Mexican president defends himself for backing PRI.

text.p: Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo on Monday defended his decision to campaign on behalf of his Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) that has stirred up a firestorm of protest from the opposition.
In a nationwide television address Zedillo not only restated his alllegiance to the PRI and applauded it for backing him, he also launched a thinly-veiled attack on the opposition.

The unusual defence, in a country where the PRI has ruled without a break for 68 years, comes from a president who on taking office in December 1994 pledged to put a "healthy distance" between himself and his party.

Opposition leaders said that policy was officially abandoned last Saturday when Zedillo told 300 PRI candidates for mid-term elections in July that he needed them to hold on to their Congressional majority to help him finish his job.

"I will continue governing for everyone, without any distinction of party militancy, but I do not agree with those who censure my right as a citizen to militate in the political party of my preference," Zedillo said on Monday night.

Though support by heads of state for their parties is the norm in most countries, in Mexico it has developed taboo status among the opposition because of a checkered electoral history in which the PRI has long been accused of using government support and funds to maintain its grip on power.
Political analysts say Zedillo has been forced to rally support for his party because of its weakened position ahead of the July elections.

In a apparent show of defiance to his critics, Zedillo on reproduced the gist of a stump-like speech he delivered on Saturday, praising the PRI for backing his emergency measures to drag Mexico out of economic crisis in 1995.

Zedillo insisted he had broken no law by addressing the PRI candidates and that he was "morally authorised" to do so. Mexico's main electoral body, the Federal Electoral Institute, endorsed the view that no law was broken over the weekend.

But opposition leaders were furious. "The president of the republic has just declared the death of the 'healthy distance'," said Carlos Castillo Peraza, the National Action Party candidate for mayor of Mexico City.
He said Zedillo had committed a "political imprudence that threatens or could threaten the transition, and democracy."
Opinion polls suggest the PRI will face one of its toughest electoral battles in July, because of a crisis in 1995 in which Mexico suffered its worst recession in 50 years.
